title: The background job that was starving the API
question: Tell me about the hardest issue you have debugged

situation: A service responsible for orchestrating and storing image functions was passed to our team, handed over by a team in the US. We then took on an ongoing project to extend it to also handle ZIP functions, after which the team started being paged 50 or more times a week, dozens of those in the middle of the night, because of API load shedding, even though our instances were heavily over-provisioned.
task: I took on finding the root cause of the resource exhaustion, stopping the pages for good, and re-architecting the system so the load shedding couldn't come back.
action: Root cause analysis: I dug into the system and found that extending it to handle high-volume ZIP functions had broken the background job architecture, which had only ever been built for image functions. Once ZIP functions came online, image functions dropped to just 10% of the total load, and the background jobs, which only ever needed to run for image functions, couldn't keep up. They were scanning the whole database daily and filtering active records locally on the host nodes.

Query and architectural refactoring: I designed a simplified querying framework keyed on entity state and targeted timestamps, so a host only fetched the records that actually needed work. I deliberately capped per-host execution under a minute, to keep long-running background work from impacting other parts of the service, like the APIs.

State sharding and rate limiting: to stay under the database partition throughput limits and avoid throttling, I introduced state sharding and rate limiting, letting several concurrent background workers each process their own dedicated shard safely.
result: API load shedding and the operational pages disappeared entirely, and background job throughput went up tenfold with dynamic scaling built in.

challenge: Diagnosing why high-priority API calls were being dropped in production. The service had only recently moved from the US to Europe, so team knowledge was thin and the existing operational metrics were poorly understood, which made it hard to pin the cause on background scans starving the API threads.
hardestBug: Realising the background jobs were impacting the API was the hard part. Each run picked a random host from the fleet and moved to a different one next time. On top of that, the issue only showed up in a handful of regions, and even there, not every day, so there was no steady signal to chase, just a pattern that had to be pieced together from limited visibility into individual job runs.
differently: I would master the service's existing telemetry and query metrics first, and build custom dashboards, before dropping into code-level debugging. Working on an inherited service without a solid grasp of its metric boundaries slowed the early diagnosis down. That's easier to say in hindsight than to do in the moment, though: with pages piling up, it takes real discipline to step back and invest in operational visibility instead of chasing the bug head-on.
aboutYourself: During one especially intense on-call week, I learned that pride was part of what kept me pushing through alone rather than asking for help sooner. Running on too little sleep while trying to fight every fire at once just isn't sustainable, and I've since gotten better at recognising when I'm stretched too thin and need to bring someone else in, rather than letting pride get in the way.
enjoyed: Watching the impact land on the CloudWatch dashboards: page volume dropping to zero, API drops flatlining, and background job throughput spiking tenfold.
